scenes.text: The first jukebox had no speakers; you listened through a tube.
It appeared on November twenty third, eighteen eighty nine, in a San Francisco saloon.
It was built by Louis Glass and his partner William Arnold.
They put an Edison electric phonograph inside an oak cabinet.
Then they added a coin slot: a nickel in the slot phonograph.
Drop in a nickel, hold the tube to your ear, and a song played from a wax cylinder.
It played one cylinder at a time, swapped by hand.
And it ran on a heavy battery weighing about twenty five pounds.
A second machine went into the same saloon just a few weeks later.
It was a hit, so Glass placed more machines in bars, restaurants and ferries.
In eighteen ninety, he claimed his machines had taken in more than four thousand dollars.
Sadly, none of those first machines are known to survive today.
In nineteen oh six, John Gabel's Automatic Entertainer offered twenty four songs.
The name jukebox caught on decades later, from juke joints where people danced.
Juke is thought to come from a Gullah word meaning rowdy.
By the nineteen fifties, America had about three quarters of a million jukeboxes.
What song would you have paid a nickel to hear?

title: The first jukebox made you listen through a tube 🎧
caption: On Nov 23, 1889, Louis Glass put a coin-operated Edison phonograph in a San Francisco saloon. No speakers: you listened through a tube for a nickel.
